results.excerpt: Her father, Wilmot, kept the lighthouse at Carrow Point. As a girl Tessaly counted the 112 steps to the lamp room every evening and wound the mechanism with him.
She met Edmund in 1962 when the Carrow ferry was delayed three hours by fog. He lent her his coat and they shared a bag of peppermints.
In 2016 she moved from the house to a second-floor flat on Quay Street with a view of the harbour mouth. She took the ship's clock and the press and little else.
At sixty she walked the Greywether coast path, 190 miles in sixteen days, with Rosalind joining her for the last three.
Her saffron buns were made with a pinch of cardamom and soaked currants and baked on Saturdays. The recipe came from her grandmother Hester.

results.excerpt: Her father, Wilmot, kept the lighthouse at Carrow Point. As a girl Tessaly counted the 112 steps to the lamp room every evening and wound the mechanism with him.
She met Edmund in 1962 when the Carrow ferry was delayed three hours by fog. He lent her his coat and they shared a bag of peppermints.
In 2016 she moved from the house to a second-floor flat on Quay Street with a view of the harbour mouth. She took the ship's clock and the press and little else.
At sixty she walked the Greywether coast path, 190 miles in sixteen days, with Rosalind joining her for the last three.
On a holiday in Port Saverne in 1983 she lost her passport on the second day and spent the rest of the week visiting the consulate. She said the consul's waiting room had the best coffee of the trip.

results.excerpt: At eighteen, in 1959, she was apprenticed at the Marlowe & Finch bindery. Old Mr Finch made her sew headbands for six months before she was allowed to touch leather.
Her most prized tool was a brass-tipped bone folder given to her by Mr Finch when she finished her apprenticeship. She would not let anyone else use it.
In retirement she taught a free bookbinding class at the town library on Tuesday mornings. Her oldest student was ninety-one.
She opened her own bindery, The Gilded Signature, on Tanner's Row in 1974 and ran it for twenty-nine years, closing in 2003.
She trained one apprentice, Corwin Hale, who started by sweeping the shop floor at sixteen. He took over her tools when she retired and sent her a hand-bound diary every December.

results.excerpt: At eighteen, in 1959, she was apprenticed at the Marlowe & Finch bindery. Old Mr Finch made her sew headbands for six months before she was allowed to touch leather.
She opened her own bindery, The Gilded Signature, on Tanner's Row in 1974 and ran it for twenty-nine years, closing in 2003.

results.excerpt: Her speciality was marbled endpapers. Her signature pattern, which she called storm tide, used indigo and rust swirled with a comb made from her mother's hat pins.
She knitted one fisherman's jumper each winter, always in undyed wool. She never followed a pattern and never made two alike.
Their daughter Rosalind was born in 1966. She became a marine biologist who studies kelp forests; Tessaly kept her first published paper in the family Bible.
Her last companion was a grey cat named Vellum, who slept in the paper drawer. Vellum came from the lifeboat station, where she had been living under the slipway.
In January 1953 a storm surge flooded the lower town. Tessaly, then eleven, spent two nights in the church hall of St Brannoc and remembered the smell of wet wool ever after.

results.excerpt: Her speciality was marbled endpapers. Her signature pattern, which she called storm tide, used indigo and rust swirled with a comb made from her mother's hat pins.
She knitted one fisherman's jumper each winter, always in undyed wool. She never followed a pattern and never made two alike.
Their daughter Rosalind was born in 1966. She became a marine biologist who studies kelp forests; Tessaly kept her first published paper in the family Bible.
In 1998 she travelled to Japan for three weeks to study suminagashi, floating-ink marbling, with a teacher named Hayato Mori. She called it the only time she felt like a beginner again.
She opened her own bindery, The Gilded Signature, on Tanner's Row in 1974 and ran it for twenty-nine years, closing in 2003.

results.excerpt: She met Edmund in 1962 when the Carrow ferry was delayed three hours by fog. He lent her his coat and they shared a bag of peppermints.
Her father, Wilmot, kept the lighthouse at Carrow Point. As a girl Tessaly counted the 112 steps to the lamp room every evening and wound the mechanism with him.
For their twenty-fifth anniversary Edmund built her a ship's clock in a walnut case. He set it four minutes fast on purpose so she would never miss the ferry.
Their daughter Rosalind was born in 1966. She became a marine biologist who studies kelp forests; Tessaly kept her first published paper in the family Bible.
Tessaly and Edmund married on 14 May 1964 at St Brannoc chapel. It rained all morning and cleared at the moment they walked out; she carried lilac from her mother's garden.

results.excerpt: She met Edmund in 1962 when the Carrow ferry was delayed three hours by fog. He lent her his coat and they shared a bag of peppermints.
Her father, Wilmot, kept the lighthouse at Carrow Point. As a girl Tessaly counted the 112 steps to the lamp room every evening and wound the mechanism with him.
Tessaly and Edmund married on 14 May 1964 at St Brannoc chapel. It rained all morning and cleared at the moment they walked out; she carried lilac from her mother's garden.
For their honeymoon they took the night train to Vessant and stayed five days. Edmund lost his hat out of the carriage window on the first evening.
For their twenty-fifth anniversary Edmund built her a ship's clock in a walnut case. He set it four minutes fast on purpose so she would never miss the ferry.

results.excerpt: She met Edmund in 1962 when the Carrow ferry was delayed three hours by fog. He lent her his coat and they shared a bag of peppermints.
Tessaly and Edmund married on 14 May 1964 at St Brannoc chapel. It rained all morning and cleared at the moment they walked out; she carried lilac from her mother's garden.
Her father, Wilmot, kept the lighthouse at Carrow Point. As a girl Tessaly counted the 112 steps to the lamp room every evening and wound the mechanism with him.
Her brother Ansel emigrated in 1960 and worked as a ship's engineer. They wrote to each other every month after they reconciled; she kept his letters in a biscuit tin.
Their daughter Rosalind was born in 1966. She became a marine biologist who studies kelp forests; Tessaly kept her first published paper in the family Bible.

results.excerpt: She met Edmund in 1962 when the Carrow ferry was delayed three hours by fog. He lent her his coat and they shared a bag of peppermints.
Her father, Wilmot, kept the lighthouse at Carrow Point. As a girl Tessaly counted the 112 steps to the lamp room every evening and wound the mechanism with him.
For their twenty-fifth anniversary Edmund built her a ship's clock in a walnut case. He set it four minutes fast on purpose so she would never miss the ferry.
Tessaly and Edmund married on 14 May 1964 at St Brannoc chapel. It rained all morning and cleared at the moment they walked out; she carried lilac from her mother's garden.
In January 1953 a storm surge flooded the lower town. Tessaly, then eleven, spent two nights in the church hall of St Brannoc and remembered the smell of wet wool ever after.

results.excerpt: Her last companion was a grey cat named Vellum, who slept in the paper drawer. Vellum came from the lifeboat station, where she had been living under the slipway.
In 2016 she moved from the house to a second-floor flat on Quay Street with a view of the harbour mouth. She took the ship's clock and the press and little else.
For their honeymoon they took the night train to Vessant and stayed five days. Edmund lost his hat out of the carriage window on the first evening.
Her speciality was marbled endpapers. Her signature pattern, which she called storm tide, used indigo and rust swirled with a comb made from her mother's hat pins.
She listened to the shipping forecast every night before sleeping. She said it was the only poetry she knew by heart.

results.excerpt: Her last companion was a grey cat named Vellum, who slept in the paper drawer. Vellum came from the lifeboat station, where she had been living under the slipway.
In 2016 she moved from the house to a second-floor flat on Quay Street with a view of the harbour mouth. She took the ship's clock and the press and little else.
At eighteen, in 1959, she was apprenticed at the Marlowe & Finch bindery. Old Mr Finch made her sew headbands for six months before she was allowed to touch leather.
She listened to the shipping forecast every night before sleeping. She said it was the only poetry she knew by heart.
Her speciality was marbled endpapers. Her signature pattern, which she called storm tide, used indigo and rust swirled with a comb made from her mother's hat pins.
